item.title: Dante Returns to Where Its New York Story Began With a New Nolita Restaurant
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Dante is returning to the place where its New York story began. This fall, Australian husband-and-wife hospitality duo Linden Pride and Nathalie Hudson will open Dante Elizabeth Street at 210 Elizabeth Street in Manhattan’s Nolita, the same address where the couple once decided to build their life and hospitality career in New York. The new restaurant brings together two defining elements of the Dante identity: a wood-fired grill and oven led by Executive Chef Daniel Garwood and an aperitivo bar built around the Italian ritual of lingering over drinks and conversation. The result is intended as a distinctly New York expression of the brand’s evolution across New York, Los Angeles and London.

Garwood’s cooking draws on his experience in Tasmania, Italy and Australia, with the open fire at the center of an ingredient-led menu designed for sharing. On the other side of the room, Pride’s cocktail program puts particular attention on the Spritz, alongside Martinis, Negronis and reinterpretations of classic cocktails. The 205-seat space, designed by Nathalie Hudson with AvroKO’s Adam Farmerie, combines a horseshoe-shaped bar, open kitchen, layered lighting and eclectic artwork, while the restaurant’s Elizabeth Street setting places it within one of downtown Manhattan’s more intimate crossroads, near the Elizabeth Street Garden, SoHo, the Lower East Side and East Village.

The Curated Take: The most compelling part of Dante Elizabeth Street is not simply that an established restaurant brand is opening another New York location. It is that Pride and Hudson are returning to the exact place where they made the decision that set their hospitality story in motion. The new restaurant therefore becomes both a homecoming and a statement about what Dante has become: an Italian-inspired New York institution that has spent a decade refining the art of the aperitivo while continuing to evolve.

item.title: In Calgary, the Restaurant Reservation Becomes the Reason to Go
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Calgary, some restaurant reservations are becoming destinations in their own right. At EIGHT, hidden inside the ALT Hotel and accessed through an unassuming phone in the lobby, just eight guests gather around the kitchen for Chef Darren MacLean’s tasting experience. The restaurant, which was ranked No. 2 on the 2026 North America’s 50 Best Restaurants list, releases reservations quarterly for a single service four nights a week. Its intimate format and focus on Canadian ingredients make the meal as much an exploration of Alberta as a night out. Next door, afterEIGHT extends the experience into a tiny speakeasy-style bar that was recognized among the World’s 50 Best Bar Openings in 2025.

Calgary’s culinary appeal also extends beyond the city table. The new Forage to Table experience takes guests to Saskatoon Farm with Chef Paul Rogalski and foraging expert Denis Manzer to gather ingredients before returning to Rouge, the historic garden-to-table restaurant, for a four-course dinner inspired by the day’s harvest. Meanwhile, newer spots including DOPO and Francine’s are adding their own distinctive energy to Calgary’s dining scene, with intimate formats and highly personal touches that have quickly made reservations part of the experience. Together, these restaurants reflect a city where Alberta’s ingredients, international influences and local stories increasingly shape the reason to visit.

The Curated Take: Culinary travel works best when the meal could only happen in that particular place. Calgary’s most compelling tables do more than serve food: they connect diners to Alberta’s landscape, ingredients, history and people. For travelers who plan journeys around what they will eat, securing the reservation may be the first step in building the itinerary.

item.title: Hilton’s 2027 Travel Trends Point to a More Personal Kind of Escape
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hilton’s 2027 Trends Report suggests travelers are beginning to let go of the idea of the perfect vacation in favor of travel that better fits their lives, interests and sense of wellbeing. Based on a Morning Consult survey of 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, the report identifies five shifts shaping the year ahead: travelers embracing “good-ish” trips on their own terms, placing greater trust in human expertise, using travel for personal growth, redefining wellness and making room for shorter, more frequent escapes. More than half of respondents, 54%, say they feel pressure to have the perfect trip, while 76% say simply having a trip on the calendar gives them something to look forward to.

Several of the findings point toward a broader redefinition of what makes travel valuable. Nearly one-third of travelers have taken a trip alone while meeting friends or family at their destination, while 42% say travel has helped them discover new interests or passions. Wellness is becoming more closely tied to nature and a sense of place, with 79% saying fresh air and the outdoors are essential to how they relax while traveling. Time is also influencing the shape of the journey: 67% favor trips that allow them to experience a lot in a short amount of time, and 63% prefer a central base with plenty to explore nearby.

The Curated Take: The most interesting idea in Hilton’s “Great Rebalance” may be the rejection of travel perfection itself. The findings suggest that travelers are increasingly valuing what a journey gives them rather than how impressive it looks from the outside. That opens space for a more personal kind of luxury, one built around meaningful experiences, trusted human guidance, restoration and the freedom to travel in ways that actually suit the individual.

item.title: The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Celebrates 10 Years Through the Story of Its Island
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort will mark its 10th anniversary this festive season by turning the story of Vommuli Island into the foundation for its celebrations. From December 20, 2026 through January 7, 2027, “Chapter X” will explore the island through four distinct ecological zones: Lagoon, Beach, Jungle and Coast. Each becomes a setting for festive dining, cultural experiences, wellness, family activities and St. Regis traditions, creating a celebration that looks beyond the resort’s anniversary to the natural and cultural character of its Maldivian setting.

The Lagoon zone draws on the surrounding marine life and overwater architecture, while the Beach zone reflects the island’s coastal heritage and connection to generations of Maldivian fishing traditions. In the Jungle, Vommuli House becomes a space for children and multigenerational families to explore local biodiversity through storytelling and nature-focused activities. The Coastal zone takes inspiration from the traditional dhoni and the Maldives’ seafaring heritage. The festive calendar will also include Christmas traditions, culinary events, wellness experiences and a New Year’s Eve celebration overlooking the Indian Ocean.

The Curated Take: An anniversary can easily become an exercise in looking backward. At Vommuli, the more interesting idea is to use 10 years as a reason to look more closely at the island itself. By organizing the festive season around its different environments and layers of heritage, the resort makes its milestone feel connected to place rather than simply to the passage of time.

item.title: Capella Sydney Deepens Its Place in the City With a Second MICHELIN Key
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Capella Sydney has been awarded Two MICHELIN Keys for 2026, becoming the only hotel in Sydney to receive the distinction this year and advancing from One MICHELIN Key in 2025. The recognition comes during a particularly strong period for the hotel, which was also named No. 16 on The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026 list and Best Hotel in Oceania for the second consecutive year. Together, the accolades reflect a property that has quickly established an identity rooted not simply in luxury, but in design, hospitality and a strong connection to Sydney.

That sense of place begins with the building itself. Capella Sydney occupies the heritage-listed former Department of Education building in the city’s Sandstone Precinct, where original architectural details are paired with contemporary Australian design and a collection of more than 1,400 artworks. Since opening in 2023, the hotel has extended that connection through its dining, wellness and cultural offerings, including Brasserie 1930, McRae Bar, Auriga Spa and its Culturists, who introduce guests to the people, places and stories that shape the city.

The Curated Take: The second MICHELIN Key is significant because Capella Sydney is no longer simply a beautifully restored historic building with a new luxury hotel inside it. The property has had several years to establish how it interprets Sydney through art, architecture, hospitality and access to the city, making this recognition feel more like an acknowledgment of an emerging Sydney institution than a debut accolade.

item.title: The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Turns Reef Restoration Into Part of the Guest Experience
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort has begun a new chapter in marine conservation with Coral RISE, a coral restoration initiative on its house reef in Baa Atoll. The first phase, completed in September, installed 100 Reef Stars carrying 1,500 coral fragments using the MARS Assisted Reef Restoration System, a science-based approach designed to provide damaged reef areas with a stable foundation for coral growth and marine habitat. The project is being developed with MARS Sustainable Solutions and will continue with monitoring and maintenance as the reef develops.

What distinguishes the initiative is its connection to the guest experience. The restoration site is accessible for snorkeling, allowing visitors to observe the Reef Stars and follow the progress of the coral over time, while marine education introduces guests to the importance of reef ecosystems in the Maldives. The project also complements the resort’s broader sustainability efforts and its location within the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve of Baa Atoll, where the surrounding marine environment is central to the destination itself.

The Curated Take: Coral RISE moves conservation from something a resort promotes to something guests can actually see taking shape. That creates a different relationship with the destination: rather than simply enjoying the reef, travelers have an opportunity to understand the work involved in helping restore it and to return to see how that effort evolves.

item.title: The Nam Hai Creates a Vietnamese Take on the Festive Season
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai in Hoi An, the festive season takes on a distinctly Vietnamese character. From December 22, 2026 through January 1, 2027, the all-villa resort will combine familiar holiday traditions with experiences rooted in Central Vietnam, from the Thap Nen candle-lighting ceremony and an Enchanted Chocolate Garden exploring Vietnam’s cacao traditions to Christmas dining and a Midnight Forest New Year’s Eve celebration beneath the tropical canopy. The setting, with private pools, gardens and views of the sea, allows families and friends to move between celebration and quiet time at their own pace.

The season also extends beyond the resort itself, with Hoi An Ancient Town, My Son Sanctuary and the Imperial City of Hue offering access to the region’s layered cultural heritage. Guests can explore Hoi An by Vespa, visit a fishing village by bamboo basket boat or incorporate seasonal wellness into their stay at the lotus-filled Heart of the Earth Spa, where new Khoi Sac treatments draw on Vietnamese traditions of renewal. Private villas, including the three-bedroom ocean-view option, provide a residential setting for multigenerational gatherings while preserving space for individual retreat.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is less about recreating a conventional Christmas in a tropical setting and more about allowing the holiday season to become part of the destination. Vietnamese rituals, Central Vietnam’s cultural heritage, local ingredients and the resort’s distinctive coastal setting give familiar celebrations a sense of place.

item.title: Hotel Mulia Senayan’s 2026 Tripadvisor Honors Span Suites and Dining
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hotel Mulia Senayan in Jakarta has earned multiple Tripadvisor Travelers’ Choice recognitions for 2026, extending across its accommodation and dining experiences. The Suites at Hotel Mulia Senayan received Travelers’ Choice Best of the Best, placing it among the top 1% of properties on Tripadvisor, while the hotel itself ranks among the top 10% of hotels on the platform. The recognition also reaches into the hotel’s culinary portfolio, with Table8 among the top 1% of restaurants worldwide and Edogin, Cascade Lounge, il Mare and The Café among the top 10%.

The breadth of the honors offers a snapshot of what has made Hotel Mulia Senayan a longstanding presence in Jakarta’s luxury hospitality scene. Located in the Senayan district near the Jakarta Convention Center and the city’s only golf course within the city center, the 994-room hotel combines extensive accommodations and event spaces with a notably broad dining program. The Suites, introduced in 2015, add a more personalized layer of hospitality through dedicated butler service and individually tailored details, while the property’s international art collection extends throughout guest rooms and public spaces.

The Curated Take: Rather than recognizing a single standout experience, Tripadvisor’s 2026 honors touch nearly every part of the Hotel Mulia Senayan experience, from its most private accommodations to its restaurants and lounge. For travelers looking at Jakarta through the lens of established luxury, that consistency across such a large property is part of the story.

item.title: 40 Years Later, Crocodile Dundee Still Sends Travelers Into the Australian Outback
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Forty years after Crocodile Dundee arrived in U.S. cinemas, the film’s influence on Australian tourism is still visible in the travelers who follow its trail into the Northern Territory. The 1986 hit transformed the landscapes of Australia into a global backdrop, with Kakadu National Park among its most recognizable locations. The film became the second-highest-grossing movie at the U.S. box office that year, behind Top Gun, while international visitor numbers to Australia doubled to more than two million annually by 1990. Its longer legacy may be the way it helped establish what is now known as set jetting, turning places seen on screen into destinations worth experiencing in person.

Kakadu remains the center of the Crocodile Dundee story, but today’s travelers can experience the landscape beyond the movie set. Self-guided itineraries and 4WD tours revisit locations associated with the film, while Yellow Water cruises offer encounters with saltwater crocodiles, waterbirds and other wildlife on the billabong. Accommodation ranges from the distinctive Crocodile Hotel to Cooinda Lodge, with the wider national park providing access to waterfalls, gorges, wetlands and Indigenous cultural landscapes that give the region its identity beyond its Hollywood connection.

The Curated Take: The enduring “Dundee effect” is an early example of something that has become increasingly powerful in travel: a story can create curiosity about a place, but the landscape has to deliver an experience worth traveling for. In Kakadu, the film provides the starting point, while the wildlife, scale and cultural depth of the Northern Territory give travelers a reason to keep exploring long after the movie reference has faded.
